However, one patient was asymptomatic (n: 1/6 = 17%). The distribution of alopecia and associated signs were diverse: areas involved ranged from patchy hair loss confined to the vertex (n: 4/6 = 67%) or also involving the parietal area (n: 1/6 = 17%) or frontal scalp (n: 2/6 = 33%), diffuse thinning by the temples (n: 1/6 = 17%), diffuse erythema without scale (n: 1/6 = 17%) or diffuse scaling (n: 2/6 = 33%) (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Mid-scalp histopathology from a case with clinicopathologic findings favoring CCCA; the bulb lymphocytic infiltrate and melanophages are supporting inflammatory findings but are not disease-specific and are also seen in alopecia areata. B: Companion mid-scalp histology panel with prominent mature lymphocytic infiltrate around and within hair bulbs; in the disease-focused CCCA case this is retained as supportive inflammatory evidence, though the pattern overlaps with alopecia areata. C: Shows focal follicular scarring with perifollicular fibrosis and an asterisk annotation, a classic histopathologic correlate of cicatricial alopecia supported by the CCCA-focused article and mid-scalp caption. D: Perifollicular lymphocytic inflammation with fibroplasia is a classic scarring-alopecia histology pattern in the mid-scalp specimen of a case in which CCCA was favored.

A: Low-power (×4) H&E histopathology of the patient's scalp biopsy showing perifollicular fibrosis and lymphocytic inflammation, explicitly captioned as consistent with central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia; real diagnostic tissue image from the index case.
